To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
greater total arterial compliance, measured as stroke volume/pulse wave velocity, was associated with a reduced rate of incident cardiovascular events.

increased total arterial compliance, as manifest by a higher ratio of stroke volume/pulse wave velocity, is associated with a lower risk for incident cardiovascular events, whereas systemic vascular resistance is not.

greater total arterial compliance, measured as the stroke volume/pulse ratio, was associated with a reduced risk of subsequent cardiovascular events in a population of individuals free of overt cardiovascular diseases at baseline, while systemic vascular resistance was not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of novel methods for the non-invasive assessment of arterial hemodynamics in humans, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and ultrasound.

the relationship between arterial function (resistive and pulsatile hemodynamics) and the risk of subsequent cardiovascular events in a population without overt cardiovascular disease at the time of study enrollment.

the development, validation, and clinical application of new imaging and computational techniques that can provide quantitative measures of vascular structure and function, with the goal of understanding the mechanisms underlying cardiovascular disease, and improving the ability to detect, diagnose, and treat patients with cardiovascular disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the relationship between resistive and pulsatile arterial hemodynamics and cardiovascular events is complex and may be dependent on the underlying population.

the relationship between arterial function, specifically total arterial compliance, and incident cardiovascular events has not been well studied in the general population, and the findings of the present study are in line with previous reports in patients with established cardiovascular disease.
the relationship between SVR (a measure of microvascular resistance) and cardiovascular events is unclear.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ratio of stroke pressure to pulse pressure, a surrogate for arterial compliance is a predictor for cardiovascular events in a population free of cardiovascular disease.

increased arterial compliance, as measured by stroke volume to pulse wave velocity (a surrogate for total arterial compliance), is associated with reduced cardiovascular disease incidence in individuals without overt cardiovascular disease.

increased arterial compliance is associated with a lower incidence of cardiovascular events in subjects without overt cardiovascular disease at enrollment, and that these findings are independent of the presence of risk factors for cardiovascular disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pulsatility of the arterial system is important in determining cardiovascular events.

the relationship between arterial function, as measured by systemic vascular resistance and total arterial compliance, and subsequent cardiovascular events is different than that previously described in populations with overt cardiovascular disease.
the ratio of stroke volumes to pulse pressure is a marker of cardiovascular risk, and this may reflect the ability of the heart and the large conduit vessels to work together.
